inScope.q: Who is the founder of Taekwon-Do?
inScope.answer: General Choi Hong Hi was the founder of Taekwon-Do. He was a general in the Korean army, born in 1918 and died in 2002. General Choi Hong Hi. He was a general in the Korean army. He was born in 1918 and died in 2002.

inScope.q: What are the five tenets of Taekwon-Do?
inScope.answer: Courtesy, Integrity, Perseverance, Self-Control and Indomitable Spirit. These are the five big ideas every Taekwon-Do student tries to live by. Courtesy is being polite and kind. Integrity is being honest and doing the right thing. Perseverance is keeping trying even when it is hard. Self-Control is staying calm and not losing your temper. Indomitable Spirit is being brave and not giving up even when you feel scared or tired.

inScope.q: What does the white belt mean?
inScope.answer: White belt means innocence, as that of a beginning student who has no previous knowledge of Taekwon-Do. Everyone starts with a white belt, and you are a beginner just starting to learn

inScope.q: What does the yellow belt mean?
inScope.answer: Yellow signifies the earth from which a plant sprouts and takes root as the Taekwon-Do foundation is being laid. Simple: yellow is the colour of the earth. Like a seed putting down roots before it grows tall, at yellow belt you practise the basics until they are strong

inScope.q: Which stance does Chon-Ji start in?
inScope.answer:
A pattern is called tul (you may also see it spelled teul). It is a set of moves done in a fixed order, as if fighting pretend opponents. ITF Taekwon-Do has 24 patterns. Chon-Ji is the first one.

Official ITF wording (NZ-HB): Chon-Ji means literally “the Heaven the Earth”. It is, in the Orient, interpreted as the creation of the world or the beginning of human history, therefore, it is the initial pattern played by the beginner. This pattern consists of two similar parts; one to represent the Heaven and the other the Earth.

Chon is Heaven (the sky above) and Ji is Earth (the ground below). It is about how everything began, so it is the first pattern you learn. It has two halves that are alike: one for Heaven and one for Earth.

Chon-Ji has 19 moves. It is the pattern you need for the grading from 9th kup to 8th kup (yellow stripe to yellow belt).

Chon-Ji starts in parallel ready stance (narani junbi sogi). The floor pattern is a cross, like a plus sign. You stand in the middle facing D (the front). A is to your right, B is to your left and C is behind you.

Moves 1 to 4:

1. Step the left foot to the left (B) into a left walking stance and do a low block with the left forearm.
2. Step forward with the right foot into a right walking stance and do a middle punch with the right fist.
3. Turn to the right (clockwise) towards A, into a right walking stance, and do a low block with the right forearm.
4. Step forward with the left foot into a left walking stance and do a middle punch with the left fist.

Moves 5 to 8:

5. Turn to face the front (D) with the left foot, into a left walking stance, and do a low block with the left forearm.
6. Step forward with the right foot into a right walking stance and do a middle punch with the right fist.
7. Turn to the right (clockwise) to face the back (C), into a right walking stance, and do a low block with the right forearm.
8. Step forward with the left foot into a left walking stance and do a middle punch with the left fist.

The second part, the part for Earth, uses L-stance for the blocks.

9. Move the left foot towards A into a right L-stance and do a middle block with the left inner forearm.
10. Step forward with the right foot into a right walking stance and do a middle punch with the right fist.
11. Turn clockwise towards B into a left L-stance and do a middle block with the right inner forearm.
12. Step forward with the left foot into a left walking stance and do a middle punch with the left fist.

In move 13 you block with the left inner forearm, and in move 15 with the right inner forearm.

13. Move the left foot towards C into a right L-stance and do a middle block with the left inner forearm.
14. Step forward with the right foot into a right walking stance and do a middle punch with the right fist.
15. Turn clockwise towards D into a left L-stance and do a middle block with the right inner forearm.
16. Step forward with the left foot into a left walking stance and do a middle punch with the left fist.

At the end, bring the left foot back to parallel ready stance.

17. Step forward with the right foot into a right walking stance and do a middle punch with the right fist.
18. Step backwards with the right foot into a left walking stance, still facing D, and do a middle punch with the left fist.
19. Step backwards with the left foot into a right walking stance, still facing D, and do a middle punch with the right fist.

End: bring the left foot back to parallel ready stance.

All the punches in Chon-Ji are middle obverse punches (kaunde baro jirugi). Obverse means you punch with the hand on the same side as your front foot: right foot in front, right fist punches. A reverse punch (bandae jirugi) uses the other hand.

inScope.q: Which foot goes back at the end of Chon-Ji?
inScope.answer: At the end of Chon-Ji, the left foot goes back to the parallel ready stance. Simple: The last step says to bring the left foot back to parallel ready stance.

inScope.q: What is the first move of Chon-Ji?
inScope.answer: Step the left foot to the left (B) into a left walking stance and do a low block with the left forearm. This is move 1 of Chon-Ji.

inScope.q: Which stance do you use for the blocks in Chon-Ji moves 9 to 16?
inScope.answer:
Sogi means stance. Attention stance is charyot sogi. Stand tall with your heels together and your toes pointing out a little, like a V. Arms down by your sides, eyes looking forward.

Parallel stance is narani sogi. Your feet are about shoulder width apart and both point straight forward, like train tracks. Parallel ready stance is narani junbi sogi: the same feet, with both fists held in front of your belt. Chon-Ji and Saju Jirugi start from parallel ready stance.

Walking stance is gunnun sogi. One foot is in front, like taking a big step. Bend your front knee, keep your back leg straight, and keep your weight even on both feet. If your left foot is in front it is a left walking stance.

Nagagi means stepping forward. Duruogi means stepping backward. We practise stepping in walking stance before we learn patterns.

L-stance is niunja sogi. Your feet make a shape like the letter L. Most of your weight is on your back leg and both knees are bent. If your right leg is at the back it is called a right L-stance. Chon-Ji uses L-stance for the inner forearm blocks.

Sitting stance is annun sogi. Your feet are wide apart and point forward, your knees bend out over your feet, and your back stays straight, like sitting on a horse. Your weight is even on both feet.

inScope.q: What does Saju Jirugi mean?
inScope.answer: Saju Jirugi is the four-direction punch. It is a practice exercise where you start in a parallel ready stance, punch while walking, then turn with a low block and punch again, until you face all four directions. You do it once starting with the right foot and once with the left

inScope.q: What is Saju Makgi?
inScope.answer: Saju Makgi is the four-direction block. It is a practice exercise. In walking stance you do a knife-hand low block, then step forward with an inner forearm middle block, and you turn so you block in all four directions. You do it once on each side. Saju Makgi is the four-direction block. It is also a practice exercise. In walking stance you do a knife-hand low block, then step forward with an inner forearm middle block, and you turn so you block in all four directions. You do it once on each side.

inScope.q: What is the Korean name for walking stance?
inScope.answer: Gunnun sogi. The Korean name for walking stance is gunnun sogi. One foot is in front, like taking a big step. Bend your front knee, keep your back leg straight, and keep your weight even on both feet. If your left foot is in front it is a left walking stance.

inScope.q: What part of the foot do you use for a front snap kick?
inScope.answer: A front snap kick is apcha busigi. Lift your knee, snap your foot out and pull it straight back. You hit with the ball of your foot (ap kumchi), so pull your toes back. For a front snap kick, you use the ball of your foot.

inScope.q: What belt comes after white?
inScope.answer: After white belt comes a white belt with a yellow stripe (9th kup), then 8th kup is yellow belt. So the next belt after white is white with a yellow stripe. White belt with a yellow stripe (9th kup) comes after white belt. Then 8th kup is yellow belt. So the belt that comes after white is the one with a yellow stripe, called 9th kup.

inScope.q: Why do I pull my toes back?
inScope.answer: Pulling your toes back helps you hit the foot with the ball of your foot and keeps the foot straight when you kick. This is part of the front snap kick.

inScope.q: What is a dobok?
inScope.answer: The dobok is the white training uniform we wear. The dojang is the training hall where we practice

inScope.q: What does kihap mean?
inScope.answer: Kihap means a yell or shout. It is a short, loud sound from your belly that helps you breathe out and put power into a move. Charyot means attention. When you hear charyot, you stand up straight in attention stance, quiet and still, ready to listen.

inScope.q: What is the Korean word for block?
inScope.answer: Makgi means block. (From the first line: "English: block Korean: makgi") The direct answer is: makgi.

inScope.q: What does ITF stand for?
inScope.answer: International Taekwon-Do Federation ITF stands for International Taekwon-Do Federation. General Choi started it in Seoul, Korea, on 22 March 1966. Our club does ITF Taekwon-Do. World Taekwondo (WT) is a different style with different patterns, so this app only covers ITF.

inScope.q: When was Taekwon-Do given its name?
inScope.answer: General Choi gave Taekwon-Do its name on 11 April 1955. That day is called Taekwon-Do's name day.

inScope.q: What does kaunde mean?
inScope.answer: Kaunde means middle, about shoulder level. Moves aim at three heights: high is nopunde (about eye level), middle is kaunde (about shoulder level), low is najunde (about belt level and below).
